title: The Retirement State

primary_metric: a state's 2017 all-cause death rate per 100,000 residents, read two ways: crude (derived: deaths / Census July 1 estimate) and age-adjusted (NCHS); the higher rate on a basis is the state that basis points the award at

options.B: Give the Fund's award to Georgia, the finalist with the higher age-adjusted death rate (The Adjusted Map)

deliverables.text: The rates table: crude and age-adjusted death rates for Florida, Georgia and the United States, with signed percent differences from the U.S.
Gaps and the age factor: Florida-Georgia gap on each basis, and crude / age-adjusted for Florida, Georgia and the U.S.
Box-and-whisker plots of the 51 jurisdictions' crude and age-adjusted rates with fences, outliers, Florida and Georgia marked, and ranks.
The earlier years: which state is higher on each basis in 2010 and 2017, with the gap as a percent of the higher rate.

appendices.title: Inputs for Florida, Georgia and the United States, 2017
Why These Two States, and What Is Out of Scope

balance.argument_a: Florida, crude basis: the rate residents actually experience is 971.4 vs 798.2 per 100,000 (17.8% higher; 12.2% above the U.S.; 17th highest of 51 vs 42nd), and anything the Fund buys that responds to deaths as they occur (hospice and home health, ambulance coverage, bereavement support) must be sized to the age mix that is actually there. The crude gap is in Florida's favor as the target in every year 2010-2017 (17.2% to 20.4%). The charter says 'death rate', not 'age-adjusted death rate'.
balance.argument_b: Georgia, age-adjusted basis: Florida has the oldest population of the 51 (20.1% aged 65+ vs 13.5%; age factor 1.445 vs 1.006), so at the same ages Georgia's rate is 793.7 vs 672.1 (15.3% higher; 8.4% above the U.S. and 13th highest vs 8.2% below and 44th). NCHS's purpose for age adjustment is comparing populations with different age structures. A prevention grant changes risk at a given age, and risk at a given age is higher in Georgia. Georgia's two readings agree (798.2 and 793.7); Florida's are 299.3 points apart.
balance.margin_basis: Gap divided by the HIGHER rate on each basis. Crude: (971.4 - 798.2) / 971.4 = 17.8%. Age-adjusted: (793.7 - 672.1) / 793.7 = 15.3%. Both inside the 20% cap; margin_pct records the larger. By the gap/lower convention these are 21.7% and 18.1% (not used).

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The weight the board puts on the crude reading versus the age-adjusted reading is a value judgment about what the grant buys, not a measurement; no amount of research can supply it, and choosing it is the case's dilemma. Flexing it +/-50% around an equal split moves the blended index from Georgia ahead (w=0.25, 7.7%) to Florida ahead (w=0.75, 11.3%); the tie is at w=0.454 (sensitivity_model.py, FACILITATOR.md).

twist.summary: Post-decision, delivered at 15:00. CDC provisional COVID-19 death rates, cumulative 2020-01-01 to 2026-09-12 (data as of 2026-09-17): Florida crude 399.6 vs Georgia 360.4 (Florida ahead by 9.8% of the higher); age-adjusted Florida 270.1 vs Georgia 342.0 (Georgia ahead by 21.0% of the higher). Each state is again above the U.S. on exactly one reading. Breaks: the 'two readings are about equally strong' symmetry (17.8 vs 15.3 becomes 9.8 vs 21.0), the equal-weight 'split the difference' blend (Florida by 1.7% becomes Georgia by 6.5%), and the 'one-year accident' reading. Does not make either lens obviously right: the crude rate still points at Florida and the charter's question is unchanged.

real_world_basis: Real data: NCHS all-cause deaths and age-adjusted rates by state (2010-2017), Census July 1 population estimates and age counts, NCHS published crude rates as a cross-check. Fictional: the Harbor Light Health Fund, its charter, its board and Lindiwe Haverstock. The shortlist of two states is a scenario choice (Appendix E gives the rule).

context_glossary.desc: A place's deaths in a year divided by the number of residents, scaled to 100,000. It is the average chance of dying for everyone who lives there, whatever their ages.
A death rate recalculated as if every place had the same mix of ages as one fixed standard population, so places with older or younger residents can be compared fairly.
A fixed, agreed-upon set of age shares (here, the U.S. population of the year 2000) that every place is adjusted to, so the comparison uses one yardstick.
The federal agency that collects and publishes U.S. death-certificate statistics, including the file this case uses.
The Census Bureau's yearly estimate of how many residents each state has on July 1, used as the denominator of a rate.

context_why_notes.D1: Why a rate per 100,000: states of very different sizes can only be compared by scaling to the same number of people, and the U.S. rate is the yardstick for 'above' and 'below'.
context_why_notes.D2: Why the age factor: dividing the crude rate by the age-adjusted rate shows how much of a state's death rate is explained by its age mix.
context_why_notes.D3: Why 51 box plots: two states' rates mean little until you see where they sit among all the others, on each of the two readings.
context_why_notes.D4: Why earlier years: a result in one year could be luck; the same order in other years shows the disagreement between the two readings is not an accident of 2017.
